item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Eritrea and Ethiopia shutter embassies as new Red Sea conflict looms
item.description:
Eritrea and Ethiopia shutter embassies as new Red Sea conflict looms

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 19:22
In response to Ethiopia's embassy closure, Eritrea accused Addis Ababa of funding armed groups to topple government
Tigray People's Liberation Front fighters walk towards a field in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 30 June 2021(Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP)
Off

Eritrea and Ethiopia have severed all diplomatic ties after accusing one another of engaging in hostile actions, in a major flare-up that could foreshadow another war on the volatile Red Sea.

Ethiopia on Thursday announced it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats and closing its embassy in Eritrea’s capital of Asmara, after reports of explosions in Addis Ababa.

The strike punctured Addis Ababa’s relative calm despite Ethiopia’s federal government battling an alliance of rebel movements opposed to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in Ethiopia’s regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar.

Western and regional officials in Addis Ababa confirmed to Middle East Eye the sound of explosions in the capital due to a drone strike. AFP reported that the explosion rocked the Ethiopian National Defence Force headquarters in the Tor Hayloch area of Addis Ababa. 

In a statement, Ethiopia accused Eritrea of engaging in “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence” against it.

Eritrea said in response it was severing all diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, accusing it of pursuing “an agenda of incessant hostility” against it. 

“In parallel with these aggressive intentions, Ethiopia has gone further to host, train, and provide arms to an assortment of what it calls ‘Eritrean armed opposition groups’ to stoke internal conflict for ‘regime change’ in Eritrea,” Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Deterioration of ties, risks

Eritrea and Ethiopia have been at odds for months, with regional diplomats warning that ties were deteriorating fast.

The two briefly formed an alliance to fight the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the ruling party in Ethiopia's Tigray region, during Ethiopia’s 2020-2022 civil war. Since then, they have returned to being bitter foes.

Addis Ababa has made claims against Eritrea’s Red Sea coastline and accuses Eritrea of supporting rebel groups like the TPLF, which Asmara denies.

"[Abiy Ahmed] has a two-waters strategy like Israel. Only for him it is from the Nile River to the Red Sea," Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh told MEE in an exclusive interview from Asmara last month. He referred to an Israeli expansionist vision that stretches from the Gaza Strip to the Jordan River at the frontier of the occupied West Bank.

With fighting already flaring between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF, a breakdown in relations with Eritrea could widen the war to the Red Sea at a time when Yemen and Sudan are both in conflict.

The risk is that the conflict could draw in regional players, including Egypt, Turkey, Somalia, and the Gulf states.

The TPLF is already aligned with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), which are fighting the Rapid Support Forces, a militia accused of genocide that is backed by the UAE and has training camps in Ethiopia. Eritrea is aligned with Egypt and Saudi Arabia in supporting the SAF.

One of Ethiopia’s staunchest supporters is the UAE, which has provided drones and other military supplies to Abiy Ahmed’s forces.

Saleh also told MEE that Asmara believes the UAE is cooperating with Israel against Asmara.

Israel has a historical precedent for supporting Ethiopia. In the late 1970s and late 1980s, Israel provided arms to Ethiopia's Marxist Derg government, which were used against Eritrean fighters.

Day after day, the Israeli-occupied village of Mansouri, perched on a green hill a few kilometres south of the coastal city of Tyre, is slowly disappearing. Already heavily damaged during the war, it is now quite literally being wiped off the map, in a final twist of cynicism, during the ceasefire.

The village, which the Israeli army presents as an operational stronghold of Hezbollah, was initially located outside the “Yellow Line”, the “security” demarcation imposed by Israel on Lebanese territory shortly after the latest ceasefire came into effect.

Even then, residents Middle East Eye spoke to following the ceasefire feared that the zone would eventually swallow up their village. It now has, although officially only in part: the Yellow Line cuts through Mansouri, dividing it in two.

On paper, that is, as the village is now entirely occupied – this summer, all the residents who had returned to the area had no choice but to flee once again, under fire from the Israeli air force, which continues its operations.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why Russia remains stubbornly insignificant to the Middle East
item.description:
Why Russia remains stubbornly insignificant to the Middle East

Submitted by Joseph Massad on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 12:45
Moscow's call for Palestinian statehood is empty rhetoric from a state that chose Israel in 1948 and stands by it today through genocide in Gaza and war on Iran
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on 26 September 2026 (Charly Triballeau/AFP)
Off

In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly last week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov emphasised: "The time has also come to address the main issue in the Middle East - ensuring the Palestinian statehood on the basis of countless United Nations decisions."

Support for Palestinian statehood has been Moscow's position since the Soviet Union backed partition in 1947, and it has remained so since the Russian Federation's establishment in December 1991.

Rather than providing the Palestinians with substantial support against their Israeli colonisers, the Russian Federation has, since 1991, at best offered nothing more than empty diplomatic rhetoric in support of a defunct two-state solution while maintaining cordial relations with Israel.

Even after Israel openly aligned itself with the all-out western war against Russia through the war in Ukraine, the Russians have not abandoned their alliance with Israel. In that alliance, and in its pretence of "both-sidesism" through continued support for the defunct two-state solution, the Russian Federation has fared much worse than the USSR.

Aside from meaningless diplomatic declarations like Lavrov's last week, Russia's lukewarm support for Iran in the current war is hardly a major deviation from the Soviets' careful balancing act in the post-war period. The Soviet and subsequent Russian commitment to alienating the Arab public continues apace.

Far from forging a new path, the Russian Federation has refused to change its policies towards the Palestinians and Zionism, except by increasing trade and security coordination with Israel over the past three and a half decades. Its support for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which collaborates with Israel and the West, hardly counts as support for the Palestinians.

Given these realities, it is curious that no one in Russia's ruling circles has thought of radically changing its failed Middle East policy.

Soviet alternatives

The Russian Bolsheviks, both Christians and Jews, had all along vehemently opposed not only Zionism but even the anti-Zionist Jewish nationalism of the General Jewish Labour Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia (known as the Bund), which called for non-territorial Jewish cultural autonomy.

It was after the Russian Revolution and the establishment of the Soviet Union that Bolshevik opposition to Zionism became state policy, while their earlier opposition to Bundist Jewish nationalism wavered. The Bund soon dissolved itself, and most of its members joined the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU).

Indeed, many former Bundists became officials in the party's Jewish Section (Yevsektsia), implementing Soviet cultural and linguistic (Yiddish) policies towards the union's Jewish population.

It was after the Russian Revolution and the establishment of the Soviet Union that Bolshevik opposition to Zionism became state policy

It was the Jewish Section of the CPSU that led the charge against Zionism in the country. Zionist organising became illegal in the USSR, and prominent Soviet Jewish and Christian figures railed against the settler-colonial movement in speeches and publications, describing Zionists as colonialists who aimed to subordinate indigenous Palestinian workers to British capital.

At the same time, the Soviets embarked on a policy that continued the tsars' sponsorship of Jewish agricultural colonisation inside the country, which dated back to the late 18th century.

Under the tsars, Russian Jews were dispatched to Siberia, southern Russia, the Caucasus and Crimea to establish agricultural settlements, a number of which were still prospering at the time of the Russian Revolution.

The onslaught of the tsarist White armies and their western European sponsors against the revolution devastated the Pale of Settlement, where most Jews had lived under the tsars, killing upwards of 100,000 Jews and destroying the livelihoods of the survivors.

It was in that context that the nascent Soviet government co-sponsored and co-financed a new project with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee to establish more agricultural colonies for Jews in southern Ukraine, the North Caucasus, the Volga region and Crimea. The project ran from 1924 until 1938, when the joint committee ran out of the funding to continue.

Soviet Zion

In 1934, the Soviets, who refused to create a "Jewish" province in Crimea because of opposition from the indigenous Crimean Tatars, created one in sparsely populated Birobidzhan. This was intended to satisfy anti-Zionist Jewish nationalists who saw the principled Soviet policies of fighting antisemitism and integrating Soviet Jews as the best riposte to settler-colonial Zionism.

While many Jewish officials opposed the project, a pro-Birobidzhan article in the Communist International's (Comintern) International Press Correspondence (Inprecor) declared:

Now proof has been furnished that the Jews, like all the other peoples, are able like pioneers, under the hardest physical conditions, to convert an undeveloped country into a country of socialist culture. There is no "Arab question", no conflict of imperialist interests, no flight from one anti-Semitism to another. That is the solution to the Jewish question by the Soviet Power.

The article, by an author identified only as MZ, was titled "Socialist Construction in the Soviet Union: Biro Bijan, an Autonomous Jewish Province" and appeared in Inprecor, volume 14, number 32, on 1 June 1934.

Indeed, it was the soft Zionist and hard anti-communist Hannah Arendt who admitted as much: "The Russian Revolution has dealt a blow to the first [Zionist] contention that the Jewish Question can be solved only in Palestine and that antisemitism is only to be eradicated by the building up of Palestine, in other words by the exodus of Jews from their former homelands."

Still, the majority of Soviet Jews remained anti-nationalist and supported assimilation into Soviet society. Only a small percentage moved to Birobidzhan or to the agricultural colonies, while the majority moved to large Soviet cities in Russia, Belorussia and Ukraine, spurning Jewish nationalism in all its guises - Zionist, Bundist and Soviet-sponsored alike.

By the Second World War, Jews were so integrated into Soviet society that more than 100 Jewish generals served during the war in the Red Army, which the Jewish Bolshevik Leon Trotsky had founded and led.

The Soviets and their Communist International defended the Palestinians' right to revolt against the British and the Zionists in both the 1920s and the 1930s, condemning the Zionists outright. In the wake of the 1929 Palestinian Buraq Wall uprising, Georgy Safarov, deputy director of the Comintern's Eastern Department, strongly condemned the "Zionist colonies in Palestine", describing "the Jewish community in Palestine [as] a British imperialist avant-garde".

By the end of the war and after the Holocaust, however, Stalin had made an about-face.

Zionist reversal

Zionist lobbying of Soviet embassies in Britain and Turkey helped, but was not the main reason. At the beginning of the Cold War, the reactionary Arab monarchies and the conservative Palestinian leadership were allied with the imperialist West. Their post-war alliances and hostility to communism did not endear them to the Soviets.

Zionist pretensions to being committed socialists and non-partisan in the Cold War helped convince the Soviets to support a one-state solution for Palestinians and Jewish settlers or, failing that, the partition of Palestine into two states - one for the settlers and the other for the indigenous population.

The Soviet ambassador to the UN, Andrei Gromyko, received new instructions from Moscow in April 1947 that upended the previous Soviet anti-Zionist position. Gromyko gave impassioned speeches in May and November 1947, defending the Jewish settlers' alleged right to establish a state in Palestine while blaming western European countries for failing to help Jews during the war.

Zionism was built as a bulwark against socialism

When Israel was proclaimed, the Soviets rushed to recognise it, earning the hostility of the majority of the Arab world and permanently alienating all Arab communist parties, which toed the Soviet line, from the Arab public. If the Soviets thought they had gained an ally in the Middle East by supporting the Zionists, they soon realised their miscalculation.

Still, under Nikita Khrushchev, who had succeeded Stalin as party leader the previous year, the Soviet legation in Israel was upgraded to an embassy in June 1954.

It was the Arab republics, however, that would prove the friendliest Arab regimes to the Soviets: Egypt from the mid-1950s, Iraq after 1958 and Algeria after 1962, followed by others.

The Soviets continued their diplomatic relations with Israel, while their support for the Arab republics remained lukewarm compared with western imperialism's support for Israel and the reactionary Arab regimes.

Israel's alliance with imperialism and hostility to the Soviets were such that it launched a campaign branding the Soviets, the first regime in the world committed to fighting antisemitism in word and deed, as "antisemites".

As Jews in western countries refused to move to Israel and immigration dried up, the Israelis sought to bring Soviet Jews to populate their settler-colony. That was the context in which they charged the Soviets with antisemitism for refusing to allow Soviet Jews to leave for Israel.

Diplomatic limits

The Soviets cut off relations with the Jewish settler-colony after the Israeli invasion of three Arab countries in 1967. Israel then intensified its campaign against Soviet "antisemitism" until the Soviets finally succumbed and allowed large-scale Jewish emigration from 1971 onwards. Half of those who left chose the US rather than Israel.

The relaxation was part of the Soviet attempt to maintain detente with the US, which led the anti-Soviet campaign on Israel's behalf. It was Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev who relaxed emigration restrictions between 1987 and 1989, allowing a million Soviet Jews to leave the collapsing USSR for Israel, the only country that would readily take them.

Gorbachev re-established diplomatic relations with Israel in October 1991, and on 16 December that year, under US pressure, the Soviet Union voted to repeal the UN's "Zionism is racism" resolution, which the Soviets had supported in 1975.

Unless it radically changes its Middle East strategy, Russia will remain an insignificant factor in the ongoing struggle to end Zionist settler-colonialism and Israeli regional imperialism

If Stalin's about-face on Zionism was motivated by the Holocaust, the Cold War and the dearth of pro-Soviet Arab rulers, would the current western war against Russia, the genocide of the Palestinians and the anti-imperialism of Iran and the Lebanese and Palestinian resistance not be sufficient to prompt another reversal?

It is true that all the Arab regimes, including the collaborationist PA, are in the West's back pocket today, as they were in 1948. They are not, however, the only players in the political field.

Western support for the Zionist project was aimed, as the antisemitic Winston Churchill put it in his 1920 article "Zionism versus Bolshevism", at striking a blow against the Russian Revolution and "international communism", which he identified as a Jewish "world-wide conspiracy".

Britain's Balfour Declaration, issued in 1917 in support of what Churchill called the "National Jews", five days before the triumph of the Russian Revolution, was engineered to prevent Russian Jewish support for the revolution. The plan failed.

Under Gorbachev, however, the Soviet Union aptly cast one of its last votes at the UN to rehabilitate Zionism. By supporting the repeal of the "Zionism is racism" resolution days before the curtain dropped on the USSR, it erased the Soviet era's anti-Zionism once and for all.

In view of this history, the Russian Federation should expect little change in its standing in the Middle East. Unless it radically changes its Middle East strategy, it will remain an insignificant factor in the ongoing struggle to end Zionist settler-colonialism and Israeli regional imperialism.

item.description:
Israel’s top court backs barring Palestinian politician from election over article

Submitted by MEE staff on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 08:47
Sami Abu Shehadeh withdraws from race after Supreme Court tells him judges are united in upholding his disqualification
(L to R) Palestinian lawmakers Yousef Jabareen,Sami Abu Shehadeh, and Ahmad Tibi attend a hearing at the Supreme Court in Jerusalem on 1 October 2026 (Ilia Yefimovich/AFP)
Off

Israel’s top court has backed barring a Palestinian politician with Israeli citizenship from standing in the upcoming parliamentary election, citing an article he wrote on 8 October 2023.

Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Balad party, withdrew his candidacy on Friday after the Supreme Court recommended he do so on Thursday.

Abu Shehadeh, a key figure in the Palestinian-majority Joint List, was disqualified from standing last month by the Central Elections Committee, a body controlled by the governing coalition.

His disqualification centred on an article he wrote in the immediate aftermath of the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel on 7 October.

The article, titled “The Al-Aqsa Flood: Preliminary Observations”, was published in Arabic by the Arab48 news outlet on 8 October 2023. It presented a preliminary analysis of the attack and its ramifications.

In it, Abu Shehadeh argued that the “unfolding strategic event” should not have come as a surprise.

“What happened and is happening, up to this moment, is entirely consistent with the law of physics that we all know: excessive pressure leads to an explosion,” he wrote.

“Decades of occupation and blockade, the assassination of leaders, the daily killing of people, and violations against the dignity, property, and holy places of the Palestinian people – all of this could only lead to a reaction.”

“The real surprise is the Palestinian people’s capacity for endurance, until they reached the point of explosion.”

Israeli election committee bans Arab parties from standing in next month's vote
Read More »

He also wrote that the attack showed that “Israel and its intelligence services are made up of human beings like us” and could “be prevented from penetrating our countries, parties, and political movements – if there is the will to do so and if we organise ourselves properly”. 

He added that for the Palestinian cause to gain politically, “the resistance must involve the Palestine Liberation Organization in all its components in the political process that the battle will open up”.

Based mainly on the article, Abu Shehadeh was accused of supporting armed struggle against Israel and denying the country’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state.

He denied both charges and appealed the decision to the Supreme Court.

He said the decision was an attempt to “undermine the representation and political voice of Arab society” in parliament, or the Knesset.

His representative, Hassan Jabareen, said the article contained no “direct call for violence, nor any statements that could amount to grounds for disqualification”.

Judges back disqualification

Supreme Court President Isaac Amit recommended on Thursday that Abu Shehadeh withdraw his candidacy, giving him until Friday to decide.

The court told Abu Shehadeh there was a consensus among the judges to uphold his disqualification, suggesting they would have barred him had he not withdrawn voluntarily.

In a statement, Balad said Abu Shehadeh had decided to step down “out of political responsibility towards our people and the Joint List, and because of the serious repercussions this could have for political and parliamentary work as a whole”.

Read More »

“Abu Shehadeh fought the legal and political battle all the way to the end against the fascist right and the Zionist consensus,” it added.

The Supreme Court is also set to review appeals against the disqualification of the Joint List and United Arab List, coalitions of parties representing Palestinians in Israel that could play a kingmaking role after next month’s elections, as well as Ofer Cassif, a Jewish lawmaker and outspoken critic of the government’s actions against Palestinians.

The Central Elections Committee, which barred Abu Shehadeh, rejected similar requests against Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism.

Both politicians have repeatedly called for actions against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank that critics and rights groups have described as violations of international law.

Ben-Gvir previously called for people in Gaza to be killed if they did not pose a threat, saying they were “not worthy of life”.

Smotrich has said that allowing two million Palestinians in Gaza to die of hunger “might be justified and moral”. He has also called for the Palestinian town of Huwara to be “wiped out”.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why Palestine solidarity activists must keep up pressure on UK government
item.description:
Why Palestine solidarity activists must keep up pressure on UK government 

Submitted by Ben Jamal on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 19:56
Miliband has announced a reset of the country's Israel policy, but the real test will be in what comes next
Protesters chant slogans and wave Palestinian flags during a demonstration against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, in central London on 8 June 2024 (Justin Tallis/AFP)
Off

One of the lines used by Zionist critics of British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement of a ban on settlement goods was that he was driven to this position by domestic considerations; that he was pandering to voters in an upcoming by-election, and to party members at Labour’s annual conference.

There is partial truth to these claims - partial because it ignores the driving factor of Israel’s increasingly naked project of aggressive colonisation of the West Bank, which has rendered increasingly untenable the UK’s policy of rhetorical support for Palestinian national rights and lack of action on Israeli expansionism. 

But it is true to the extent that Labour’s desire for a reset was propelled by the party’s loss of support among voters angered by the Starmer government’s complicity in the Gaza genocide. 

That anger, shared by a large segment of the Labour party, had been made clear at the party’s conference last year when a motion, recognising the genocide and calling for action to end the UK complicity and a full arms embargo, was passed with overwhelming backing.

So if that membership was part of the audience Miliband wanted to appease with his reset, then he will be pleased at the response he received on the conference floor. 

The loudest cheers came in a passage when he directly addressed the millions who have protested on the streets for three years telling them: ”you were right”, an appeal designed to reach way beyond the hall to the movement which has driven public opinion on this issue through sustained protest, to reassure us ”don’t worry we get it - we, like you, are now on the right side of history.”

Other actions, besides the speech, were designed to send a similar message. Most notably, the historic decision not to send a single cabinet minister to The Labour Friends of Israel reception, as Miliband embraced the Palestinian Ambassador publicly at the Labour Friends of Palestine event.   

All of these steps, alongside the substance of the settlement ban, as I have written previously, should be welcomed. However, they must be seen and responded to as initial steps on a long overdue journey, the floor of what is required not the ceiling.

Miliband wrapped the reset on Palestine within a framework of Labour internationalism. 

In a key passage of his conference speech, he made reference to Labour’s historic role in developing institutions such as the UN, designed to ensure that the horrors of the Holocaust would never be repeated and that states would abide by international law.  

“Fighting for those values of democracy, the rule of the law, protection for rights and freedoms, is essential to tackle injustice and suffering,” Miliband said.

Undoubtedly fine words. But living up to that commitment in relation to Palestine, and achieving a true moral and material reset, demands more than what has been offered so far. It requires a fundamental shift away from key aspects of the framing within which the settlement trade ban has been promised.

Targeting occupation 

Miliband has been keen to stress that the actions he has introduced are targeting the illegal occupation, but not Israel itself - a state with which the UK wishes to retain close relations. Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty has emphasised this point, noting that his government’s quarrel was with the Netanyahu administration, not with Israel or the Israeli people. 

This narrative rests on the belief that Israel is a liberal democracy undertaking an illegitimate occupation that is not supported by the majority of its people. But these assumptions are false. 

The occupation is supported by every party with a chance of forming government, and opinion polls show widespread public support for such policies, with more than 80 percent backing the expulsion of all Palestinians from Gaza.  

Crucially,  as numerous human rights bodies have made clear, Israel is not a democracy in relation to its treatment of the Palestinians, but a state practicing apartheid, in the words of B’Tselem, Israell’s leading human rights monitoring body, enacting a “system of Jewish supremacy from the Jordan river to the Mediterranean sea”.

Miliband says Labour is renewing its commitment to challenging global injustices. But challenging an injustice begins with naming and understanding it

Miliband says those who have protested in unprecedented numbers against the Gaza genocide for three years “were right”. But what drove us all to the streets was not merely anger at the government’s hesitation to call for a ceasefire, nor was it solely a push for action against illegal settlements. 

Rather, it was a recognition of a key truth: Israel’s genocide was built on the foundations of a system of racial supremacy that has existed for decades, with the full support of successive UK governments. 

Miliband asserts that the only path to peace and justice is via a two-state solution. But other solutions exist, including a single democratic state that respects the rights of all; it is for the Palestinian people, and not any external government, to decide which option prevails. Any solution in line with international law cannot leave intact Israel’s system of apartheid. 

Miliband says Labour is renewing its commitment to challenging global injustices. But challenging an injustice begins with naming and understanding it. 

Part of the reset being offered is a shift in the government’s response to the question of whether a genocide has been committed in Gaza. This is a welcome move away from former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s overt denial, to a position that effectively acknowledges the threshold might have been reached, while leaving the matter for international courts to determine. 

Full accountability 

As a statement of full support for the processes currently underway at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), this is welcome. But what is missing is the crucial recognition that the ICJ has already invoked obligations on all states to act to prevent genocide. 

They mirror the recommendations laid out by a special UN commission, whose findings were formally accepted by Labour members last year.

The map of the requirements was laid out in that 2025 conference motion -  a ban on settlement goods which is now promised but must be fully enacted including action against Israeli banks providing services to settlements; a full arms embargo including F35 components; and end to all trade that supports Israels illegal actions.

But further necessary steps were not addressed in that motion.

One relates to accountability, which must be extended beyond support for measures against Israel in international courts, to targeting acts of complicity by UK ministers. A recent Channel 4 broadcast outlined the ministerial manoeuvrings that enabled the continuation of arms sales to Israel during the war on Gaza. 

Miliband speaks of a Middle East policy shift - so it's time to pick a side
Read More »

Demands by former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and others for a full public enquiry into UK complicity have clear legitimacy. But events at the recent Labour conference, where hundreds of people protested the proscription of Palestine Action, focused attention on another priority: ending the repression of demonstrations for Palestinian rights. 

The Starmer government cracked down on national marches, leading to charges against several leaders of the movement and the conviction of the Stop the War Coalition’s vice chair, Chris Nineham, and myself. It doubled down with further repressive laws, giving police powers to ban protests on the grounds of “cumulative” impact and vicinity to religious sites. This legislation must be repealed. 

Journalist Omar El Akkad wrote that one day, everyone will have always been against Israel’s genocide. 

I have always taken the view that we should welcome those who recognise past errors and seek to atone and change. But that requires a commitment to genuine and full change. While Miliband’s first steps are welcome, he and the party will be judged not by what they have done so far, but by what they do next. 

We know the recent shift resulted from pressure by the solidarity movement. The same will apply to what comes next. We must keep the foot on the pedal, beginning by ensuring that the National March for Palestine on 10 October, marking three years of genocide, once again draws hundreds of thousands of people - who have indeed got it right - onto the streets.
